snapshot.capital_scaled: ₹50 lakh–2 crore for certification, production and a B2B sales team
snapshot.distribution_note: Institutions, fleets and dealers buy; certification opens doors

tailwinds: Mandatory BIS rules for helmets and other safety products push out low-quality imports.
Companies, factories and fleets must meet safety rules.
Smart devices with alerts and tracking add value.
Families pay for personal safety and elder-care devices.
headwinds: Cheap, uncertified products still sell widely.
Institutions buy slowly and through tenders.
Device failures can have serious consequences and liability.
angle_2026: Safety products are increasingly regulated, which favours certified Indian makers. In 2026, safety device businesses grow by selling to institutions that must comply, such as factories, fleets and schools, and adding smart features that make safety measurable.
cost_basis: Estimated for a brand developing one certified safety product and selling to institutions and consumers, 2026 prices.

unit_economics.note: Institutional orders can be large but need certificates, demonstrations and patience.

investor_probes: Who buys, and how long does it take?
What happens if the device fails?
How is it different from cheaper options?
bootstrap_takeaway: Certify one product, win a few institutional buyers with demonstrations, and use their references to reach more.
licences: BIS certification where mandatory (for example, helmets and fire extinguishers)

hard_truths.title: Liability
hard_truths.text: If a device fails, consequences can be serious. Insure and test thoroughly.

hard_truths.title: Cheap competitors
hard_truths.text: Uncertified products undercut you. Sell to buyers who need compliance.

plan_goal: The aim is a certified product and first orders from 3 institutional buyers.

plan.title: Validate
steps: Talk to 20 buyers about safety problems.
